title: Tri State Buffer: 7 Essential Rules for Safe Bus Sharing
text:
Digital Electronics

 Tri State Buffer: 7 Essential Rules for Safe Bus Sharing

 A normal logic output always drives the wire high or low, so two outputs on one wire will fight. A third, disconnected state lets many chips take turns on the same bus line without damage or corrupted data.

 
 High Z Output 
 Enable Pin 
 74HC125 
 74HC245 
 Bus Contention 
 




 Data buses, memory chips and SPI devices all depend on outputs that can step aside. This guide explains how a tri state buffer creates the high impedance state, how to avoid bus contention and how to size pull resistors.


 
 Hello everyone, today we are going to learn how a tri state buffer works, what the high impedance state really means and how to use enable pins, transceivers and pull resistors on a shared bus.


 
 
 
 What Is a Tri State Buffer?


 A tri state buffer is a logic buffer whose output can be high, low or high impedance, also called Z or the off state. When its enable input is active it copies the input to the output, and when disabled it electrically disconnects from the wire, as if it were not there at all.


 An ordinary logic gate has only two output states, and it always drives one of them. That is fine for point to point wiring, but a shared data line needs a way for each chip to stop driving when another chip is talking.


 
 
 Image credit: Build Electronic Circuits . Pinout courtesy of Build Electronic Circuits, shown here for educational reference. 
 

 The pinout above is the 74HC125, a quad buffer with one enable per gate. Build Electronic Circuits shows the four output enable pins on pins 1, 4, 10 and 13, and notes that the HC version runs from 2 V to 6 V while the older 74LS125 needs 5 V.

 How the High Impedance State Works


 Inside a CMOS output there is a P channel MOSFET to the supply and an N channel MOSFET to ground. For a high output the top transistor is on, for a low output the bottom one is on, and in the Z state both are switched off together.


 With both transistors off, the pin only shows a tiny leakage current and a few picofarads of capacitance. Nexperia specifies an off state output current of plus or minus 0.5 µA at 25 °C for the 74HC125, rising to plus or minus 5 µA over the industrial range up to 85 °C.


 
 
 Enable nOE Input nA Output nY Meaning 

 L L L Buffer active, drives low 

 L H H Buffer active, drives high 

 H X Z Disabled, high impedance 

 



 This function table comes from the Nexperia 74HC125 datasheet, where X means the input does not matter. The small circle on the enable pin in the symbol shows that the enable is active low.


 Do You Know?
 TRI STATE was originally a registered trademark of National Semiconductor for its three state logic products. Engineers now use the generic names three state, tri state and high Z for the same function.



 Active Low and Active High Enable Types


 
 74HC125 Quad Buffer
 Four buffers, each with its own active low enable.
 Best for: single line control and level isolation
 Active Low 

 74HC126 Quad Buffer
 Same pinout idea, but each enable is active high.
 Best for: logic where a high signal means talk
 Active High 

 74HC244 Octal Buffer
 Eight buffers in two groups of four, each group with one enable.
 Best for: driving 8 bit address or data buses
 Bus Driver 

 74HC245 Transceiver
 Eight bidirectional channels with a direction pin and an enable.
 Best for: two way data buses
 Bidirectional 




 The choice between active low and active high usually depends on the chip select logic. Many decoders produce active low outputs, which suit the 74HC125 and 74HC244 directly without extra inverters.


 Every tri state buffer in these families has the same input logic levels as other HC parts. If you mix supply voltages, check the levels described in TTL vs CMOS logic families before connecting the bus.


 Sharing a Bus Without Collisions


 On a shared bus, every device output goes through a tri state buffer, and a control circuit makes sure only one enable is active at a time. This is how a microcontroller reads memory, input ports and peripherals over the same 8 data lines.


 
 Address Decoded Logic selects one device

 One Enable Active Only that buffer drives

 Others in Z All other outputs float

 Data Read Receiver latches the value

 Enable Removed Bus is released for the next device




 The receiving device normally captures the bus value with a clock edge in a latch or register. The data must be stable before that edge, so the enable time of the buffer is part of the timing budget.


 Quick Tip
 Draw a simple timing chart of every enable signal before building a bus. If two enables overlap even for a few nanoseconds, add a small gap between one device releasing the bus and the next device driving it.



 Bus Contention and Why It Damages Chips


 Bus contention happens when two outputs drive the same line at the same time with opposite levels. One output tries to pull the line high while the other pulls it low, so a large current flows straight from the supply to ground through both output stages.


 The line sits at some middle voltage that neither receiver can read reliably, and the output transistors heat up. Short events cause supply noise and ground bounce , while long events can permanently damage the drivers.


 Common causes are overlapping chip selects and firmware that drives a pin while an external tri state buffer is also enabled. Nexperia lists about 15 ns typical enable and disable time for the 74HC125 at 4.5 V.

 Floating Bus Lines and Pull Resistors


 When every tri state buffer on a line is disabled, nothing drives the wire and it floats. A floating CMOS input can drift into the middle region, where both input transistors conduct partly, current rises and noise causes random switching.
